nameStory: "Petty spurge" gets its name from the Old French word "petit," meaning small, referring to its diminutive size compared to other spurges. The "spurge" part comes from the Latin "expurgare," meaning "to purge," because many plants in this family were historically used as purgatives. It's also called "radium weed" because of its milky sap's caustic properties.
description: Petty spurge is a small, delicate annual weed that rarely grows taller than your hand. This tiny European immigrant has smooth, pale green stems that branch out in a sprawling pattern, creating small mats in gardens and disturbed soil. Its most distinctive feature is the milky white sap that oozes from broken stems or leaves. The plant produces tiny, inconspicuous flowers clustered at the stem tips, followed by small three-part seed capsules.

idTips.label: Milky Sap
idTips.description: Break a stem and watch white, latex-like sap immediately ooze out - this milky juice is the spurge family's calling card and can irritate skin, so wash hands after touching

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves with smooth edges that feel soft and slightly succulent, arranged alternately up the stem with no visible leaf stalks

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers clustered in small umbrella-like arrangements at stem tips, so small you might miss them without looking closely

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that spreads outward more than upward, forming small patches with multiple branching stems radiating from the base

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Three-chambered seed capsules that pop open when ripe, shooting tiny gray seeds several feet away with an audible snap

habitat: Look for petty spurge in disturbed soils like garden beds, sidewalk cracks, cultivated areas, and waste ground throughout New England. It thrives in rich, loose soil and seems to appear wherever humans have been digging or gardening. This opportunistic weed particularly loves the edges of vegetable gardens and flower beds where soil is regularly turned.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as tiny rosettes with their characteristic oval leaves, beginning their rapid growth as soil warms.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their inconspicuous flowers, with the milky sap most abundant and easiest to observe during active growing season.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and explosively scatter seeds, while older plants begin yellowing and preparing to die with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants are completely dead and gone, but seeds lie dormant in soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Petty spurge's seed capsules are tiny botanical cannons that can shoot seeds up to 6 feet away with enough force to make an audible popping sound - you can actually hear a patch of them firing seeds on a quiet day!
confusionNotes: Petty spurge might be confused with other small garden weeds like chickweed or purslane, but the instant milky sap test settles any confusion - break a stem and if white latex doesn't immediately appear, it's not a spurge.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "milkweed" in some regions, petty spurge is completely unrelated to true milkweeds (Asclepias species) and shouldn't be confused with them. The milky sap of spurges can cause skin irritation and eye damage, so always wash hands after handling any spurge species.
compareHints: Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species. Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the reddish spots on spotted spurge, petty spurge has plain green oval leaves. It's much smaller than the dramatic caper spurge and lacks the creeping, mat-forming habit of the sandmat spurges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
